questions.stem:
A 3-year-old unvaccinated girl recovered from a febrile illness with a descending rash that began at her hairline and was preceded by cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Over the following year she has three hospital admissions, for bacterial pneumonia, severe diarrhea, and otitis media with mastoid involvement. Before the illness she had rarely been sick. Researchers studying such children find that the variety of memory lymphocytes in the blood is sharply reduced after the illness compared with before it.

Which of the following best explains this child's repeated infections?
choices: Persistent viral replication in the anterior horn of the spinal cord
Loss of pre-existing immune memory caused by the viral infection
Toxin-mediated activation of a large fraction of T cells
Destruction of red cell precursors through the P antigen receptor
Latent virus reactivating in sensory nerve ganglia

explain.html: Measles does more than cause an acute rash and fever: it damages the immune system itself. The virus erases previously built immune memory, a state called immune amnesia, that can last up to a year in fully recovered patients and raises susceptibility to sometimes severe secondary infections. That is why the majority of measles-associated deaths and complications are due to secondary infections such as pneumonia, diarrhea, and TB, and why pneumonia, diarrhea, and otitis media are among the most common complications. This child had measles (descending rash after cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis), then a year of bacterial pneumonia, severe diarrhea, and complicated otitis, with a sharp drop in the variety of memory lymphocytes. That pattern is lost immune memory, not a new pathogen-specific defect. Vaccination against measles therefore protects against much more than one disease.
why: Destruction of anterior horn motor neurons is the lesion of poliovirus and causes flaccid paralysis, not repeated infections.
Superantigen activation of T cells drives the acute cytokine storm of toxic shock, not a year of infections with lost memory cells.
The P antigen is the parvovirus B19 receptor on erythroid precursors, and its injury causes anemia, not recurrent infections.
Latency in sensory ganglia belongs to varicella zoster virus and causes shingles, not broad loss of immune memory.
explain.takeaway: Measles causes immune amnesia, wiping out pre-existing immune memory, so most measles deaths and complications come from secondary infections in the months after recovery.
explain.topic: Measles: immune amnesia and secondary infection
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old woman who recently moved to the US and has no vaccination records has had 2 days of low-grade fever. A fine pink maculopapular rash began on her face and spread to her trunk within a day. She has tender postauricular and suboccipital lymph nodes, and a few petechiae are seen on the soft palate. One week later the rash is gone, but she reports pain and stiffness in the small joints of both hands and both wrists. A pregnancy test is positive.

The virus causing her illness most likely belongs to which group, and what is the main concern for her pregnancy?
choices: Enveloped RNA togavirus; congenital infection of the fetus during viremia
DNA parvovirus; fetal anemia leading to hydrops fetalis
Enveloped RNA paramyxovirus; subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
Double-stranded DNA herpesvirus; latent infection of fetal nerve ganglia
Nonenveloped RNA enterovirus; fetal meningitis and encephalitis

explain.html: Rubella is a mild disease in adults caused by an enveloped RNA togavirus (genus Rubivirus). It spreads by the respiratory route, replicates in the nasopharynx and regional nodes, and becomes viremic 5 to 7 days later. After about 14 days of incubation it gives a low-grade fever, a diffuse macular and papular rash that moves from head to trunk and lasts about 3 days, postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, and sometimes petechiae on the palate. Adult women often develop polyarthralgia or polyarthritis, which is exactly what this woman reports in her hands and wrists after the rash fades. The danger is the pregnancy: the placenta and fetus are infected during the maternal viremia, causing congenital rubella syndrome, which is why unvaccinated, immigrant, and traveling women of childbearing age matter so much.

Varicella zoster is the latent herpesvirus, and its rash is vesicular in crops, not fine and macular.
Coxsackievirus causes hand, foot, and mouth disease with oral ulcers and palm and sole vesicles, not a descending rash with postauricular nodes.
explain.takeaway: Rubella (togavirus) is mild with postauricular and suboccipital nodes and arthralgia in adult women; its main danger is congenital rubella syndrome from fetal infection during maternal viremia.

questions.stem:
A 9-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a 1-minute generalized seizure. For 3 days she has had abrupt fever to 39.8 C (103.6 F) with no other symptoms. This morning the fever broke, and a few hours later a rosy-pink blanching rash appeared on her trunk, neck, and arms. She now appears well and is playful. She has occipital lymphadenopathy. Her vaccines are up to date.

After a primary infection, the virus responsible remains latent in which of the following, with a risk of severe reactivation after a stem cell transplant?
choices: Sensory nerve ganglia
Hepatocytes
Erythroid progenitors
Lymphocytes and monocytes
Anterior horn neurons

explain.html: Roseola (exanthem subitum) is a mild illness of infants 6 to 19 months caused by human herpesvirus 6, a double-stranded DNA virus. Its timing is the signature: an abrupt high fever above 103 F for 2 to 3 days, sometimes with a febrile seizure, and then a rosy-pink rash that appears after the fever subsides, mostly on the torso, neck, and arms, often with cervical and occipital nodes. This infant had 3 days of fever, a seizure, and a rash only after defervescence, and now looks well, which is classic. Seroprevalence approaches 100% by age 2, and after primary infection the virus is shed in saliva and remains latent in lymphocytes and monocytes. In immunocompromised patients, especially HSCT transplant recipients, it can reactivate and cause severe disease such as encephalitis of the temporal lobe and hippocampus or marrow suppression.
why: Sensory nerve ganglia are where varicella zoster virus hides and reactivates as shingles.
Hepatocytes are not a site of HHV-6 latency.
Erythroid progenitors are the target of parvovirus B19, not a latency site for HHV-6.
Anterior horn neurons are destroyed by poliovirus, which does not cause a fever-then-rash illness.
explain.takeaway: Roseola (HHV-6) gives several days of high fever, sometimes a febrile seizure, then a rash after defervescence; HHV-6 stays latent in lymphocytes and monocytes and can reactivate after stem cell transplant.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the temporal course of various fever and rash syndromes in pediatrics

rows.if_right: a child with chickenpox whose virus later reactivates along a dermatome

rows.if_right: a hepatitis virus that replicates in the liver

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation works as a kindergarten teacher. Three weeks ago several of her students had bright red cheeks, and she developed mild fever and painful swelling of both wrists and knees that has since resolved. A routine ultrasound now shows fetal ascites, pleural effusions, and skin edema. Doppler flow in the fetal middle cerebral artery is markedly increased, consistent with severe fetal anemia.

Which of the following best explains the fetal findings?
choices: Direct viral infection of fetal erythroid precursors and myocardial cells
Maternal antibodies crossing the placenta to destroy fetal red cells
Placental infection during viremia causing congenital cataracts
Toxin released into maternal blood that crosses the placenta
Latent viral infection established in fetal sensory ganglia

explain.html: Parvovirus B19 targets cells that carry the P antigen. Erythroid progenitors carry it, and so do fetal myocardial cells. When a woman is infected during pregnancy, the virus reaches the fetus and injures both: it halts red cell production, causing fetal anemia, and it directly damages the heart, causing myocardial dysfunction. Severe anemia plus a failing heart produce fluid in several compartments, which is hydrops fetalis. Here the clues line up: a kindergarten teacher exposed to children with slapped cheeks, her own polyarthropathy (the adult form of parvovirus infection), and now a fetus with ascites, effusions, skin edema, and Doppler evidence of severe anemia.
why: Maternal antibodies destroying fetal red cells is an alloimmune process, not the result of a viral illness caught from children.
Congenital cataracts belong to congenital rubella syndrome, and rubella does not cause slapped cheeks.
Parvovirus B19 is not toxin mediated; the damage comes from direct infection of target cells.
Latency in sensory ganglia is a property of varicella zoster virus, and parvovirus does not cause hydrops that way.
explain.takeaway: Maternal parvovirus B19 infection causes hydrops fetalis by infecting P antigen bearing fetal erythroid precursors (anemia) and myocardial cells (myocardial dysfunction).
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old unvaccinated boy has had 3 days of low-grade fever and an itchy rash. It began on his scalp and face and is now concentrated on his trunk. On examination, red papules, clear vesicles on a red base, and crusted lesions are all present side by side in the same area. New crops appeared each day. His grandmother, who lives with the family, had a painful band of blisters along one side of her chest 2 weeks ago.

Which of the following best describes the virus causing this boy's illness?
choices: A DNA poxvirus whose lesions all appear in the same stage at once
An RNA enterovirus transmitted mostly by the fecal-oral route
A DNA herpesvirus that stays latent in sensory nerve ganglia
An RNA paramyxovirus that leaves behind an immune amnesia
A DNA herpesvirus that stays latent in B lymphocytes

explain.html: Varicella zoster virus is a DNA herpesvirus that enters through the respiratory tract or conjunctiva, replicates locally and in regional nodes, then spreads in a primary viremia to organs and sensory ganglia and in a secondary viremia to the skin. After a mild 1 to 2 day prodrome, chickenpox gives a vesicular rash that starts on the head, concentrates on the trunk, and arrives in successive crops with lesions in several stages. That mix of stages separates it from variola and mpox, where all lesions are in the same stage. After the primary infection the virus persists as a latent infection in sensory ganglia and can reactivate as herpes zoster (shingles), painful blisters along one dermatome. This boy's papules, vesicles, and crusts side by side, and his grandmother's recent dermatomal blisters, fit exactly.

Enteroviruses cause hand, foot, and mouth disease with oral ulcers and palm and sole lesions, not crops on the trunk.

explain.takeaway: Varicella zoster virus, a DNA herpesvirus, causes crops of lesions in different stages (unlike smallpox and mpox) and stays latent in sensory ganglia, reactivating as shingles.

questions.stem:
A 2-year-old girl who attends daycare is brought in during August because she has refused to eat or drink for a day. Two days ago she had fever, poor appetite, and a sore throat. Now she has painful shallow ulcers in the back of the mouth and small red spots that have become gray vesicles on her palms, soles, and buttocks. Several children in her daycare room have similar symptoms.

The most likely cause of this illness has which of the following features?
choices: Enveloped DNA virus spread through sexual contact
Toxin-producing bacteria colonizing the throat
Nonenveloped RNA virus spread by the fecal-oral route
Enveloped RNA virus spread by respiratory droplets only
Tick-borne bacteria that replicate inside endothelial cells

explain.html: Non-polio enteroviruses, including coxsackievirus, are RNA viruses and the leading cause of exanthematous disease. They are ubiquitous, spread by the fecal-oral route, show a summer and fall predominance, are detected by PCR, and can also cause meningitis or encephalitis. Coxsackievirus A16 is the most common cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease in the US. The illness starts with fever, poor appetite, malaise, and sore throat; 1 to 2 days later painful sores appear in the back of the mouth (herpangina), and small red spots blister and ulcerate on the palms and soles, sometimes the knees, elbows, buttocks, or genitals. This toddler in an August daycare outbreak has posterior oral ulcers, refusal to eat, and vesicles on her palms, soles, and buttocks, the textbook picture.

Group A streptococcus causes pharyngitis and scarlet fever with a sandpaper rash, not palm and sole vesicles.

Tick-borne endothelial infection is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, with a rash that turns petechial and spreads from the wrists and ankles.
explain.takeaway: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (posterior oral ulcers plus palm and sole vesicles) is caused mainly by coxsackievirus A16, an RNA enterovirus spread fecal-orally with a summer and fall peak.

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has had 2 days of fever to 39.0 C (102.2 F) and painful swallowing. This morning his mother noticed a rough rash that started on his abdomen and spread to the trunk and limbs. It feels like fine sandpaper and is accentuated as red lines in the skin creases of the elbows. His cheeks are flushed with pallor around the mouth, his conjunctivae and lips are normal, and his tongue is red with enlarged papillae. A rapid antigen test of a throat swab is positive.

The rash is caused by which of the following, and which drug is first line?
choices: Exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein-1; clindamycin
Erythrogenic exotoxin acting as a superantigen; penicillin
Hemagglutinin binding to endothelial cells; vitamin A
Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 from the throat; vancomycin
Bacterial invasion of vessel endothelium; doxycycline

explain.html: Scarlet fever occurs most often with group A streptococcal pharyngitis, usually in children aged 4 to 8. The rash and fever are caused by erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxin, which also acts as a superantigen, driving T cell proliferation and cytokine release. The sequence is sore throat and fever, then a diffuse, palpable, sandpaper-like eruption that starts on the abdomen and spreads, accentuated in the skin creases as Pastia lines, with a strawberry tongue, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, and fine desquamation in recovery. Normal conjunctivae and lips separate it from Kawasaki disease. This boy has every feature plus a positive rapid antigen test, which confirms the diagnosis, and penicillin is the treatment.

TSST-1S. aureusSuperantigen: links TCR beta region to MHC class II outside the grooveStaphylococcal TSS
Exfoliative toxins A and BS. aureusCleave desmoglein-1 in stratum granulosumSSSS
Erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxin AGroup A strepSuperantigen; rash and feverScarlet fever, streptococcal TSS

Hemagglutinin is a measles surface protein, and vitamin A is given in measles, not in a bacterial throat infection.
TSST-1 is a staphylococcal toxin that causes shock with hypotension and multiorgan failure, not pharyngitis with a sandpaper rash.
Endothelial invasion with a petechial rash from the wrists and ankles is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, treated with doxycycline.
explain.takeaway: Scarlet fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis; erythrogenic exotoxin causes the sandpaper rash with Pastia lines and strawberry tongue, and penicillin is first line.

explain.objective: Develop ability to identify and distinguish the major “fever and rash” syndromes in pediatric patients

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man cut his forearm on a fence 2 days ago. He now has fever, severe pain in the forearm out of proportion to its appearance, and dusky, swollen skin around the cut. Blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg and creatinine is rising. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are beta-hemolytic. A surgeon finds necrotic tissue along the fascia.

In addition to surgery and supportive care, which regimen best matches this illness?
choices: Penicillin alone, since group A streptococci remain fully sensitive to it
Doxycycline, started before any confirmatory test
Intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose oral aspirin
Rifampin for 4 days for the patient and household contacts
Penicillin plus clindamycin, with intravenous immunoglobulin

explain.html: Toxic shock can be staphylococcal or streptococcal, and the two differ in setting and severity. The streptococcal form follows cuts, burns, or bruises rather than tampons, more often brings severe pain and tissue necrosis, has bacteremia in about 60%, and carries a mortality of 30 to 70%, compared with 3% for the staphylococcal form. Group A streptococcal exotoxins act as superantigens and drive a massive release of IL-1, IL-2, interferon gamma, and TNF-alpha that causes shock. Treatment uses anti-streptococcal antibiotics including one that inhibits protein synthesis, such as clindamycin, to shut down toxin production, and IVIG is added for the group A streptococcal form. This man has pain out of proportion after a fence cut, necrotic fascia, shock, rising creatinine, and beta-hemolytic chains in the blood.

Doxycycline is the empiric drug for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, not streptococcal toxic shock.
Immunoglobulin with aspirin is the treatment for Kawasaki disease, a vasculitis of young children.
Rifampin for contacts is prophylaxis against Haemophilus influenzae type b, not treatment of streptococcal shock.

explain.objective: Understand the role of targeting empiric therapy for bacterial fever and rash syndromes

questions.stem:
A 2-year-old boy had crusting around his nostrils for 3 days, then developed low-grade fever, irritability, and tender red skin. Within a day, the top layer of skin on his neck, armpits, and groin began peeling off in sheets, and light rubbing of normal-appearing skin causes it to slide off. His mouth and eyes are not involved. A culture from the nose grows Staphylococcus aureus; a culture of a blister is sterile.

The skin findings are caused by a toxin that targets which of the following?
choices: Collagen of the dermal-epidermal junction
Desmoglein-1 in the granular layer of the epidermis
Keratin filaments of basal epidermal cells
Endothelial cells of small dermal blood vessels
T cell receptors and MHC class II molecules

explain.html: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is a toxin-mediated disease: Staphylococcus aureus infecting the nose or mouth releases exfoliative toxins A and B, which circulate and act at a remote site. The toxins target desmoglein-1, so the hallmark split is in the stratum granulosum, high in the epidermis, and gentle rubbing lifts the skin away (Nikolsky sign). Clinically there is low-grade fever, then a rapidly evolving exanthem as the top layer of skin peels in sheets, with generalized exfoliation in newborns. Because the cleavage is so superficial, it heals with no scarring. This toddler had nasal crusting, then tender skin that sloughs in sheets, a positive Nikolsky sign, spared mucosa, and a sterile blister, exactly what a distant toxin predicts. Treatment is an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic plus a protein synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin, with pain control and hydration.

ToxinOrganismActionDisease

why: A split at the dermal-epidermal junction would be deeper and would scar; this cleavage is high in the epidermis.
The basal layer is not where the split happens in this disease.
Small vessel endothelium is the target of Rickettsia rickettsii in Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
Binding T cell receptors and MHC class II is the superantigen action of toxic shock toxins.
explain.takeaway: In staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, circulating exfoliative toxins A and B cleave desmoglein-1 in the stratum granulosum, giving superficial peeling with a positive Nikolsky sign and no scarring.

explain.objective: Learn to describe various skin lesions in fever and rash syndromes

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old college student has abrupt fever, chills, severe leg pain, and cold hands and feet. Within hours, a macular rash becomes petechial and then purpuric over the legs, and his blood pressure falls. Blood cultures grow an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that ferments maltose and glucose. He has had two prior episodes of similar invasive infection with the same organism. Workup for an underlying cause is planned.

Which underlying condition is most likely in this patient?
choices: Deficiency of a late complement component (C5 to C9)
Deficiency of the complement inhibitor C1 esterase
Absent thymus with low T cell numbers
Selective deficiency of IgA in mucosal secretions
Defective NADPH oxidase activity within neutrophils and monocytes

explain.html: Neisseria meningitidis is an oxidase-positive aerobic gram-negative diplococcus that ferments maltose and glucose; serogroups B, C, and Y cause most US illness. It colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads through respiratory and throat secretions, and invasive infection causes meningococcemia, meningitis, or both, with an abrupt onset of fever, chills, myalgia, limb pain, and a rash that moves from macular to petechial to purpura, sometimes with DIC and death. Risk factors for invasive disease are late complement deficiency, asplenia, and close contact with a case. The late components form the membrane attack complex that lyses Neisseria, so a patient with repeated invasive episodes, like this student on his third, points to a C5 to C9 deficiency. Each episode is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin, droplet isolation for 24 hours, and treatment of contacts.
why: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not recurrent Neisseria infection.
An absent thymus with few T cells causes viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, not a selective Neisseria pattern.
IgA deficiency gives mild mucosal infections, not recurrent meningococcemia.
NADPH oxidase defects cause abscesses with catalase-positive organisms, not repeated Neisseria sepsis.
explain.takeaway: Recurrent invasive Neisseria infection points to late complement (C5 to C9) deficiency; acute meningococcemia is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin, droplet isolation, and contact prophylaxis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

rows.why: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not recurrent Neisseria infection.
rows.if_right: recurrent episodes of facial and airway swelling without hives

rows.why: An absent thymus with few T cells causes viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, not a selective Neisseria pattern.
rows.if_right: an infant with recurrent viral and fungal infections and low T cell counts

rows.why: IgA deficiency gives mild mucosal infections, not recurrent meningococcemia.
rows.if_right: repeated sinus and lung infections with low secretory IgA

rows.why: NADPH oxidase defects cause abscesses with catalase-positive organisms, not repeated Neisseria sepsis.
rows.if_right: recurrent abscesses and pneumonias from catalase-positive bacteria and fungi

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old girl has had 5 days of fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. She now has a diffuse rash, red conjunctivae, red swollen lips, and confusion, and her blood pressure is 80/45 mm Hg. Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated, and an echocardiogram shows reduced ventricular function. Her family had a respiratory illness confirmed as COVID-19 about 4 weeks ago; she had only a mild cough at the time. Throat and blood cultures are negative.

Which of the following best describes the illness in this child?
choices: A primary viral infection of the skin by a herpesvirus
A postinfectious inflammatory syndrome that follows COVID-19
A superantigen toxin released from a tampon or wound
An acute infection of the brain caused by measles virus
A tick-borne bacterial infection of small vessel endothelial cells

explain.html: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) is a rare postinfectious condition that typically appears more than 2 weeks after COVID-19, often after a mild initial infection. It causes diffuse inflammation of the heart, lungs, kidneys, brain, skin, eyes, and gut. Persistent fever is universal, GI symptoms occur in 60 to 100%, and rash, conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, and neurocognitive symptoms are common. It can present as a severe shock-like illness with features of Kawasaki disease or toxic shock syndrome, which is why it belongs in the fever and rash differential. This girl has 5 days of fever with prominent GI symptoms, rash, red eyes and lips, confusion, shock, and reduced ventricular function 4 weeks after a household COVID-19 illness, with negative cultures and no toxin source.
why: No primary herpesvirus skin infection explains multiorgan inflammation and shock weeks after COVID-19.
Toxic shock needs a toxin-producing staph or strep source such as a tampon or wound, and none is present.
Measles encephalitis follows a measles illness with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever requires tick exposure and gives a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles.
explain.takeaway: MIS-C is a postinfectious multisystem inflammatory syndrome appearing more than 2 weeks after COVID-19, with fever, GI symptoms, rash, and shock that can mimic Kawasaki disease or toxic shock syndrome.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Develop ability to identify and distinguish the major “fever and rash” syndromes in pediatric patients

rows.why: No primary herpesvirus skin infection explains multiorgan inflammation and shock weeks after COVID-19.
rows.if_right: a vesicular rash in crops from varicella zoster virus

rows.why: Toxic shock needs a toxin-producing staph or strep source such as a tampon or wound, and none is present.
rows.if_right: a menstruating adolescent with a retained tampon, or a necrotic wound with streptococci

rows.why: Measles encephalitis follows a measles illness with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots.
rows.if_right: an unvaccinated child with a recent descending rash and Koplik spots who becomes confused

rows.why: Rocky Mountain spotted fever requires tick exposure and gives a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles.
rows.if_right: a recent camping trip with a petechial rash spreading from the wrists and ankles

questions.stem:
A 14-month-old boy is admitted in April with 4 days of fever to 40.0 C (104 F), harsh cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes that make him squint in room light. Yesterday a purple-red maculopapular rash appeared at the hairline and behind the ears and has since spread to the face and trunk. He has not received any vaccines because of family preference. Examination of the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars shows tiny white spots on a red base.

In addition to supportive care, which of the following should this child receive?
choices: Oral acyclovir for 5 days
Vitamin A supplementation
Intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin
Intravenous penicillin G
Oral azithromycin for 5 days

explain.html:
Measles is a highly contagious single-stranded RNA paramyxovirus (genus Morbillivirus) that spreads by the respiratory route, replicates in the nasopharynx and regional nodes, and seeds the tissues through two viremias. After a 10 to 12 day incubation it produces fever with the classic triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, then a maculopapular rash 3 to 5 days later that starts at the hairline and behind the ears and spreads down the trunk. Koplik spots, tiny white spots with a red halo on the buccal mucosa, are the pathognomonic enanthem. This child has every piece: high fever, the triad with photophobia, a descending rash, Koplik spots, and no vaccines.

There is no specific antiviral, and most measles deaths come from secondary infections during the immunosuppression that follows. Outcomes are better with vitamin A supplementation, so any child admitted with measles in the US should receive it, which is the one targeted therapy here.
explain.table:
FeatureKawasaki diseaseScarlet feverMeasles
ConjunctivaeBilateral, nonexudativeNormalConjunctivitis with cough and coryza
MouthStrawberry tongue, red cracked lipsStrawberry tongue, circumoral pallorKoplik spots
ExtremitiesEdema and erythema of hands and feetDesquamation in recoveryNot a feature
TreatmentIVIG and aspirinPenicillinSupportive care, vitamin A
why: Acyclovir is the antiviral for varicella zoster virus, and measles is an RNA paramyxovirus with no specific antiviral.
Immunoglobulin with aspirin treats Kawasaki disease, which lacks cough, coryza, and Koplik spots.
Penicillin treats group A streptococcal scarlet fever, a sandpaper rash after pharyngitis, not a viral exanthem with Koplik spots.
Azithromycin is an antibacterial that does nothing for a viral illness like measles.
explain.takeaway: Measles (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, descending rash) has no specific antiviral; hospitalized children receive vitamin A, which lowers complications and death.

explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

questions.stem:
A 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought in for fatigue and pallor. Ten days ago he had a low-grade fever and mild malaise, followed by bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on his arms. His younger sister had the same facial rash last week.

[[labs 0]]

The drop in hemoglobin is best explained by viral entry into which cells, using which receptor?
choices: Mature red cells, through the hemagglutinin binding site
Erythroid progenitors, through the P antigen (globoside)
Monocytes, through the complement receptor CR1
Splenic macrophages, through Fc receptors on their surface
Hepatocytes, through the bile acid transporter on the cell surface

explain.html: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): a mild prodrome, then a slapped-cheek rash and a mild peripheral macular rash that coincides with IgM in serum and signals clearance of viremia. Its key biology is a unique tropism for erythroid progenitor cells: the virus needs the P blood group antigen (globoside) to enter and is cytotoxic to pronormoblasts and normoblasts. In a healthy child the brief halt in red cell production goes unnoticed. In a patient with a hemolytic anemia such as sickle cell disease, whose red cells survive only days, the halt causes a transient aplastic crisis. This boy has a slapped cheek after a sibling exposure, hemoglobin far below his baseline, and reticulocytes near zero with normal white cells and platelets, which isolates the failure to red cell production.
why: Mature red cells are not the target; the virus kills precursors, which is why reticulocytes disappear.
Monocytes are not the parvovirus B19 target, and losing them would not stop reticulocyte production.
Increased splenic destruction would push the reticulocyte count up, not down to near zero.
Hepatocytes are not infected by parvovirus B19, and liver injury would not produce isolated reticulocytopenia.
explain.takeaway: Parvovirus B19 enters erythroid progenitors through the P antigen (globoside) and kills them, causing transient aplastic crisis with reticulocytopenia in patients with hemolytic anemia.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

rows.if_right: a hemolytic process that destroys circulating red cells and raises the reticulocyte count

rows.why: Monocytes are not the parvovirus B19 target, and losing them would not stop reticulocyte production.
rows.if_right: a virus that stays latent in lymphocytes and monocytes, such as HHV-6

rows.why: Increased splenic destruction would push the reticulocyte count up, not down to near zero.
rows.if_right: hemolysis with a brisk reticulocytosis and a large spleen

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department on day 3 of her menstrual period with sudden high fever, vomiting, watery diarrhea, and muscle aches. She is confused. Temperature is 39.6 C (103.3 F), pulse 150/min, and blood pressure 72/40 mm Hg. She has a diffuse sunburn-like erythema, red conjunctivae, and a red tongue. A tampon is removed from the vagina. Creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL (0.5 to 1.1) and platelets are 80,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Blood cultures are negative.

The toxin responsible for this illness causes disease by which of the following mechanisms?
choices: Linking T cell receptors to MHC class II outside the groove
Cleaving the protein that holds skin cells together in the epidermis
Forming pores that lyse red cells and leukocytes in the bloodstream
Blocking release of inhibitory neurotransmitters in the spinal cord
Being presented as a peptide within the MHC class II groove

explain.html: Toxic shock syndrome is a diffuse inflammatory response with fever, rash, hypotension, and multiorgan involvement caused by toxins of Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococcus. The major staphylococcal toxin is TSST-1, a superantigen. Instead of being processed and presented as a peptide in the groove, it cross-links the beta region of the T cell receptor to MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells outside the antigen-binding site, so a huge fraction of T cells fire at once and release overwhelming amounts of cytokines. The result is sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgia, a sunburn-like erythroderma, conjunctival hyperemia, strawberry tongue, and rapidly progressive organ failure. This tampon-using adolescent with shock, renal injury, low platelets, and negative blood cultures (bacteremia is low in the staphylococcal form) has staphylococcal TSS.
explain.table:
ToxinOrganismActionDisease
TSST-1S. aureusSuperantigen: links TCR beta region to MHC class II outside the grooveStaphylococcal TSS
Exfoliative toxins A and BS. aureusCleave desmoglein-1 in stratum granulosumSSSS
Erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxin AGroup A strepSuperantigen; rash and feverScarlet fever, streptococcal TSS
Hemolysins, leukocidinS. aureusLyse red cells, destroy leukocytesLocal tissue damage
Enterotoxins A to ES. aureusVomiting and diarrheaFood poisoning
why: Cleaving the protein that holds epidermal cells together is the action of exfoliative toxins in scalded skin syndrome.
Hemolysins and leukocidin lyse cells locally but do not trigger a body-wide cytokine storm with shock.
Blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release is the action of tetanus toxin, which causes rigidity and spasms.
A peptide in the MHC class II groove activates only the rare matching T cell clone; superantigens bypass the groove.
explain.takeaway: TSST-1 is a superantigen that cross-links the T cell receptor beta region to MHC class II outside the peptide groove, activating many T cells and causing a cytokine storm with shock.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes

rows.if_right: superficial skin peeling in sheets with a positive Nikolsky sign and only low-grade fever

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old boy in Oklahoma is brought in during June with 3 days of fever, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, and sensitivity to light. He went camping last week. Today small pink blanching macules appeared on his wrists and ankles, and some are becoming petechial and spreading toward his trunk; a few are on his palms.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the best next step in management?
choices: Send serology and begin treatment if titers rise
Begin oral amoxicillin and recheck in 48 hours
Give a third-generation cephalosporin and place in droplet isolation
Wait to see whether the rash reaches the palms fully
Begin doxycycline now, before any confirmatory result

explain.html: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative intracellular bacterium that multiplies in the endothelial cells of small vessels, causing thrombosis, capillary leak, edema, and petechiae. A prodrome of fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and photophobia comes first; the classic rash begins on day 2 to 5 as blanching macules on the wrists and ankles, turns petechial, spreads centripetally, and eventually reaches the palms and soles. Labs show leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and mild transaminitis. Most cases occur April to October in boys under 15 in the South Central US, matching this camper in Oklahoma in June. The disease can progress to necrosis and death, the classic rash is absent in 10 to 15%, and so therapy is empiric doxycycline right away, without waiting for serology or the full rash.

FeatureRocky Mountain spotted feverMeningococcemia
OrganismRickettsia rickettsii, intracellular gram negative, tick borneNeisseria meningitidis, gram negative diplococcus, respiratory secretions
RashWrists and ankles, blanching then petechial, spreads centripetally to palms and solesMacular, then petechial, then purpura within hours
SettingApril to October, South Central US, outdoor exposureClose contact; late complement deficiency, asplenia
TreatmentEmpiric doxycycline at onceThird generation cephalosporin, droplet isolation 24 hours, treat contacts
why: Waiting for serology delays treatment of a disease that can kill quickly; doxycycline must be empiric.
Amoxicillin does not reliably treat rickettsial infection, and a 48-hour wait is dangerous.
A third-generation cephalosporin with droplet isolation is the plan for meningococcemia, which lacks tick exposure and a wrist-ankle start.
Waiting for the classic rash is a known pitfall, since 10 to 15% of patients never develop one.
explain.takeaway: Suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever (tick exposure, wrist and ankle rash spreading centrally, low platelets and sodium) is treated with doxycycline at once, before any confirmatory test.
explain.topic: Rocky Mountain spotted fever: empiric doxycycline
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the role of targeting empiric therapy for bacterial fever and rash syndromes

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has had fever to 39.5 C (103.1 F) for 6 days and is very irritable. He has bilateral red conjunctivae without discharge, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous rash accentuated in the diaper area, swelling and redness of his hands and feet, and one enlarged node on the left side of his neck. Group A streptococcal testing is negative.

[[labs 0]]

Prompt treatment with which therapy is given mainly to prevent which complication?
choices: Penicillin, to prevent rheumatic fever and valve damage
Doxycycline, to prevent vasculitis-related gangrene
Vitamin A, to prevent pneumonia and encephalitis
Immunoglobulin with aspirin, to prevent coronary aneurysms
Clindamycin with immunoglobulin, to prevent multiorgan failure

explain.html: Kawasaki disease is a febrile exanthematous medium vessel vasculitis of unknown cause; 80% of cases are in children under 5. The diagnosis is made after 5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 features: bilateral nonexudative bulbar conjunctival injection, oral changes (strawberry tongue, red cracked lips), a polymorphous rash often exaggerated in the groin, extremity changes (induration and erythema of the hands and feet), and unilateral cervical lymphadenitis. Supporting labs include sterile pyuria, leukocytosis with a left shift, transaminitis, low albumin, and high inflammatory markers. This boy has 6 days of fever, all five features, sterile pyuria, and low albumin. If untreated, about 20% of children develop coronary artery abnormalities including aneurysm, so an echocardiogram is obtained at presentation and treatment is high-dose IVIG with aspirin.

FeatureKawasaki diseaseScarlet feverMeasles
ConjunctivaeBilateral, nonexudativeNormalConjunctivitis with cough and coryza
MouthStrawberry tongue, red cracked lipsStrawberry tongue, circumoral pallorKoplik spots
ExtremitiesEdema and erythema of hands and feetDesquamation in recoveryNot a feature
TreatmentIVIG and aspirinPenicillinSupportive care, vitamin A
why: Penicillin treats group A streptococcal infection, and his strep test is negative.
Doxycycline treats rickettsial disease, which brings a petechial rash after tick exposure.
Vitamin A is given in measles, which would have cough, coryza, and Koplik spots.
Clindamycin with IVIG is for streptococcal toxic shock, which brings hypotension and a toxin-producing infection.
explain.takeaway: Kawasaki disease (5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 mucocutaneous criteria) is treated with IVIG and aspirin to prevent the coronary artery aneurysms seen in about 20% of untreated children.
explain.topic: Kawasaki disease: treatment and cardiac risk

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old kindergarten teacher at 16 weeks' gestation calls her obstetrician. One of her students, a 6-year-old girl, was absent last week with low-grade fever and malaise, returned feeling well on Monday, and on Wednesday developed bright red cheeks and a lacy, faint rash on her arms. The girl's serum drawn on the day the rash appeared is positive for virus-specific IgM. The school nurse wants to send the girl home until the rash fades so the teacher is not exposed. The teacher has never had a slapped-cheek illness that she knows of.

Which statement best explains the timing of the girl's rash and what it means for the teacher's exposure?
choices: The rash is direct viral killing of skin cells, so it is contagious on contact
The rash signals the start of infection, so the teacher has not been exposed yet
The rash comes with antibody as viremia clears, so the exposure was last week
The rash marks peak viremia, so the girl is most contagious until it fades
The rash marks a second viremia, so she stays contagious for 4 more days

explain.html:
Viral exanthems differ in when the rash appears relative to viremia, and that timing decides when a patient is contagious. In measles the patient is most contagious from 4 days before to 4 days after the rash. In parvovirus B19 erythema infectiosum, a mild prodrome of fever and malaise is followed by a slapped-cheek rash with a lacy peripheral distribution that corresponds to the appearance of IgM in serum and signals clearance of viremia, so the rash is an immune event after the infectious phase. Parvovirus spreads by contact, fomites, and large droplets during viremia, and because fetal erythroid precursors and myocardial cells express the P antigen, maternal infection can cause fetal anemia and hydrops fetalis.

This girl was viremic during last week's prodrome, and her positive IgM on the day of the rash fits the virus clearing. Sending her home until the rash fades does nothing for the teacher, whose exposure happened during the prodrome, and the obstetric follow-up should be planned around that exposure.
explain.table:
IllnessRash relative to viremiaContagious period
Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19)Rash appears with IgM as viremia clearsProdrome, before the rash
MeaslesRash during secondary viremia4 days before to 4 days after rash
VaricellaRash after secondary viremia, crops of vesiclesUntil lesions have crusted
why: The rash corresponds to the IgM response, not virus destroying skin cells; parvovirus targets erythroid progenitors.
The rash comes after the prodrome, late in infection, so exposure has already occurred.
The parvovirus rash comes as viremia clears, so the child is past her most contagious time.
Contagiousness for 4 days after the rash is the measles rule; in parvovirus the rash follows clearance of viremia.
explain.takeaway: In parvovirus B19 erythema infectiosum, the rash appears with IgM as viremia clears, so transmission happens during the prodrome, before the rash.
explain.topic: Parvovirus B19: rash timing versus viremia
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the temporal course of various fever and rash syndromes in pediatrics

questions.stem:
An 11-year-old boy in Tennessee is brought in during July with 4 days of fever, headache, vomiting, and sensitivity to light. He hiked in the woods 9 days ago. On day 3, small pink blanching macules appeared on his wrists and ankles; they are now petechial and have spread to his arms, thighs, trunk, palms, and soles. His hands and feet are mildly swollen, and his neck is slightly stiff.

[[labs 0]]

If treatment is delayed, which development is most expected as this illness progresses?
choices: Sheets of superficial skin peeling away at the granular layer
Joint pain in the fingers and wrists lasting weeks
Dilation of the coronary arteries, with aneurysms forming
Spreading purpura with necrosis and gangrene of the digits
Profound anemia from a halt in red cell production

explain.html:
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne illness caused by the gram-negative intracellular bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii, most common April to October in boys under 15 in the South Central US. After exposure the bacteria multiply within endothelial cells of small vessels and disseminate in the bloodstream, and the endothelial cell injury leads to thrombosis and capillary leak, which produce edema and petechiae. The classic rash starts on days 2 to 5 as blanching macules on the wrists and ankles, becomes petechial, and spreads centripetally to the arms, thighs, trunk, and finally the palms and soles. Typical labs are leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, mild transaminitis, hyponatremia, and mild CSF pleocytosis, and severe cases develop DIC and necrosis.

This boy's photophobia, stiff neck, and CSF cells can pull toward meningococcal disease, but the CSF shows no organisms and only mild pleocytosis, and the rash's wrist-and-ankle start after a hike defines RMSF. One endothelial process explains the swollen hands and feet, the petechiae, and the low platelets, and if treatment is delayed the same thrombosis and leak progress to widespread necrosis, purpura, gangrene, and death. That is why doxycycline is started on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation or the classic rash.

why: Peeling at the granular layer comes from staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein-1.
Weeks of small-joint pain after a rash fit rubella or parvovirus in adult women.
Coronary aneurysm follows untreated Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis, not rickettsial endothelial infection.
A halt in red cell production is parvovirus B19 entering erythroid progenitors, not a rickettsial complication.
explain.takeaway: RMSF is endothelial infection of small vessels by Rickettsia rickettsii; untreated, thrombosis and leak progress to purpura, necrosis, gangrene and DIC, so doxycycline is started empirically.
explain.topic: Rocky Mountain spotted fever: predicting progression from the endothelial mechanism
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize associated symptoms and significance of the major “fever and rash” syndromes
